# Constellation Energy (CEG) — a deep dive on management and the setup

Forensic review of five consecutive management calls (May 2025, August 2025, November 2025, the March 2026 business and earnings outlook, and May 2026) against the reported financials and the tape as of 4 August 2026. Price used throughout: **$268.73 (US dollars, Nasdaq listing)**, a live quote taken today; the stock is down about 35% from its 52-week high of $412.70 and sits roughly 18% above the 52-week low of $228.63 set on 1 July 2026.

---

## 1. Narrative arc

The story management told changed shape three times in fifteen months, and the change is the most useful thing in the transcripts.

**Phase one (May 2025) — proving the pricing model.** The chief executive, Joe Dominguez, spent his prepared remarks arguing that Constellation does not need a data centre physically bolted onto a power plant to get paid well for its electricity. His words: the company "weren't sure about that at the beginning of this strategic effort," and had worried that fair pricing "might only be available in behind-the-meter transactions." By that call he declared himself "now convinced" that pricing works either way. This is a genuine thesis expansion — it widens the addressable customer set from the handful of sites with adjacent land to the whole regional grid.

**Phase two (August–November 2025) — the promise of a large deal.** Here the narrative narrowed onto a single un-named transaction. In August 2025 Dominguez reached for a baseball metaphor: "we're in the late innings on one transaction. We're past the seventh inning stretch." In November 2025 he repeated it almost verbatim — "That remains true, and we continue to progress" — while adding, with unusual candour, that "some of the later innings can seemingly drag out." Alongside this he added a genuinely new and, in my view, under-appreciated claim: the buyer had matured. "Today, we're seeing a far more sophisticated and aggressive customer walk through our door. They have done deals."

**Phase three (March–May 2026) — retreat to the numbers.** At the March 2026 outlook the deal did not arrive. Dominguez said it plainly: "I recognize that the last time we spoke, I indicated that we expected to be done with an important transaction by this call, but we're not ready to announce anything today." The narrative was rebuilt on arithmetic instead of anticipation — a stated 20% compound annual growth rate in base earnings through 2029, a commitment to at least 10% growth on a rolling three-year basis thereafter, a free-cash-flow outlook of $8.4 billion across 2026–2027 rising to $11.5–13 billion across 2028–2029, and a buyback authority lifted to $5 billion.

That is the arc: from *can we price it*, to *the big one is coming*, to *stop waiting for the big one, here is the baseline*. Growth drivers quietly dropped along the way include behind-the-meter co-location, which by August 2025 had become "a longer-term option" with the admission that "what we're working on right now is all front of the meter." Drivers quietly added include natural gas and geothermal (through the Calpine acquisition), nuclear power uprates — squeezing more megawatts out of existing reactors — and, most recently, a venture stake in small modular reactor developer Blue Energy announced on 16 July 2026.

---

## 2. Claims versus financials

| Management claim | Where said | What the numbers show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| Calpine "was worth twice as much as what we paid for it" | May 2025 | Deal closed 7 January 2026 at roughly $16.4 billion of equity value ($4.5 billion cash plus 50 million shares), about $26.6 billion including assumed debt. Return on invested capital for the trailing twelve months is 3.8% and return on capital employed 5.9% — low, on a capital base that just stepped up by the size of the acquisition. | **Unproven and self-serving.** One quarter of Calpine earnings sits in the numerator against a full step-up in the denominator, so the low return is partly a timing artefact. The narrative is *richer* than the trajectory in one specific place — the un-signed large contract — and *poorer* than the trajectory in another: management barely marketed the PJM capacity auction, which on 14 July 2026 cleared at the regulated ceiling of $325 per megawatt-day for the third consecutive time. That is real, dated, contracted revenue for the 2028/2029 delivery year across a large slice of the fleet, and it arrived while the stock was near its low.

---

## 3. Tone and confidence trajectory

**Rating: Stable, with a marked shift from anticipation to evidence.**

- May 2025 — offensive and expansive: "we're seeing a very, very favorable environment." Specificity about deals: low. Confidence: high.
- August 2025 — peak anticipation. "We're past the seventh inning stretch. We've song take me out to the ballpark on that one." Also the most quotable overreach of the whole sequence: "clean and reliable megawatts are the most important energy commodity in the world today."
- November 2025 — the metaphor is recycled and hedged: "some of the later innings can seemingly drag out." Simultaneously the market claim escalates: "the market is hotter now than ever." That combination — softer on the specific, louder on the general — is the classic tell that a promised event is slipping.
- March 2026 — the tone breaks. Management stops selling anticipation and starts selling arithmetic, and does so with an explicit acknowledgement of the missed promise. Guidance specificity rises sharply: a three-year growth rate, a rolling growth commitment, a two-period free-cash-flow forecast, a named buyback authority.
- May 2026 — steady and operational. "Right now, our focus is on execution." Two plants placed in service in the quarter with named capacities and locations.

There is no shift into defensive cost-and-macro language. There is a shift from *offensive about the future* to *offensive about the installed base*, which is a healthier place to be arguing from.

---

## 4. Guidance credibility

**Reliability score: Medium-High.**

What they delivered:
- The Crane Clean Energy Center restart (the former Three Mile Island Unit 1) was *pulled forward*, not pushed back — from 2028 to the second half of 2027, announced August 2025. Dominguez: "people were skeptical that we would restart in 2028. They were right to be skeptical. We're going to start it in '27."
- The Calpine acquisition closed, having been guided to close by end-2025 and completed on 7 January 2026. Approximately on time.
- The 2026 earnings guidance range of $11 to $12 per share was set in March 2026 and affirmed in May 2026.
- Two named projects entered service on schedule in the first quarter of 2026: the 105 megawatt Pastoria solar project and the 460 megawatt Pin Oak Creek gas peaking facility.
- Earnings have beaten expectations in five of the last seven quarters, roughly 71%.

What they missed:
- The large data-centre contract, promised as near-complete in August 2025 and still unannounced in May 2026. Four quarters of slippage on the single item the market cared most about.

The pattern is not sandbagging. Management sets deliverable operational dates and hits them; it sets no date at all on commercial negotiations and then narrates progress. The failure mode here is narrating a negotiation as though it were a schedule.

One structural caution for anyone reading the headline earnings line: reported accounting earnings and the adjusted figure management guides to diverge violently, because the hedge book is marked to market each quarter. First quarter 2026: $4.49 reported against $2.74 adjusted. First quarter 2025: $0.38 reported against $2.14 adjusted. The reported number is noise. Judge this company on adjusted operating earnings and on cash flow.

---

## 5. Analyst pressure points

**The deflection, repeated.** Every call, an analyst asks where the large deal stands; every call, management declines. Paul Zimbardo of Jefferies in May 2025: "is it a fair expectation that kind of you're pretty close to a deal?" Answer: "I don't want to touch that." In August 2025 the same question produced the baseball metaphor. Analysts who kept pushing were vindicated — the deal did not arrive, and the stock lost about 35% of its value in the first half of 2026.

**The question that later became bad news.** In May 2025 Angie Storozynski of Seaport asked about "quite a dramatic pullback" in forward power prices in Northern Illinois and whether data centres were shifting away from the state. Dominguez dismissed the state-specific reading. She was pointing at the right thing from the wrong angle: the risk was not Illinois politics, it was that forward power prices and the location of demand are both less settled than the narrative implied.

**The question analysts are asking that management is not fully answering.** In November 2025 Storozynski asked whether rival announcements were "more equivalent to LOIs than firm take-or-pay power contracts." Dominguez answered about customer interest, not about contract structure: "I feel that what we have and what we're offering outcompetes just about any other opportunity in the space." He never addressed the distinction. That distinction — a letter of intent versus a binding take-or-pay contract — is the whole game in this sector, and management chose not to draw it even when handed the chance.

**Where management gave a genuinely useful answer.** In May 2026 Nicholas Amicucci of Evercore asked how much of the uprate programme is inside the 2029 plan. Chief financial officer Shane Smith: "None of the uprates. The capital is out the door, but nothing is showing up as EPS accretion in '29. 2030 is the earliest that they'll add to EPS." That is the opposite of capacity inflation — spending disclosed, benefit explicitly excluded from the plan. Credit where due.

---

## 6. Red flags and green flags

**Red flags**

- *Serial slippage on the flagship commercial catalyst* (August 2025 through May 2026). Four quarters of "late innings" language with nothing signed at that scale. This is the sector's characteristic failure, and it happened here.
- *Refusal to distinguish binding contracts from framework agreements* (November 2025), when directly invited to.
- *Self-marking the Calpine acquisition at twice cost* (May 2025). Promoter language in an otherwise measured executive.
- *Grid readiness, not plant readiness, is the binding constraint on the Crane restart.* PJM identified transmission upgrades running to roughly December 2030 or later. This was materially mitigated on 1 June 2026 when the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission granted a waiver permitting the transfer of 760 megawatts of capacity interconnection rights from the retired Eddystone plant to Crane — but it took a regulatory exception, not an engineering fix, and that is a precedent that can be litigated.
- *Plaintiff-firm securities investigations announced 7–8 April 2026*, following the share-price decline. These are routine after a large drawdown and no complaint of substance is evidenced in the materials; note it, do not weight it heavily.
- *Free cash flow of $1.14 billion over the trailing twelve months* against a promise of roughly $4.2 billion a year. Explainable by growth spending, but unproven.
- *Data caveat, not a management flag:* the screening feed reports a gross margin of 75.8% and expanding. That figure is corrupted — the fourth-quarter 2025 filing feed carries a negative cost of revenue of $10.25 billion and a gross profit of $15.70 billion on $5.46 billion of revenue, an accounting-tagging artefact around the acquisition. Do not use the reported gross margin for this name. Use operating cash profit margin, which is clean and expanding.

**Green flags**

- *This company is not a serial diluter* — the opposite. The share count went from 313 million to 359 million entirely through the 50 million shares issued as acquisition currency for Calpine. The 11 million share offering priced at $281 on 1 June 2026 was a *secondary* sale by Calpine's former owners; Constellation received no proceeds and simultaneously bought stock back. Add a $5 billion repurchase authority and $735 million of actual repurchases across 2025–2026. For a sector where the standard playbook is issuing equity into a narrative, this is a meaningful differentiator.
- *Dated, named commercial wins did keep landing* while the flagship deal slipped: a 20-year agreement with Meta covering more than 1,100 megawatts at the Clinton plant (announced 2025); a carbon-free energy agreement with Comcast (August 2025); a federal government agreement (January 2025); and on 23 June 2026 a first-of-its-kind agreement with Walmart for approximately 176 megawatts from the Dresden plant, including 30 megawatts of new uprate capacity, across two fifteen-year terms beginning in 2029 and 2030.
- *Licence extension work is real and filed*: applications lodged 26 June 2026 to run the Ginna and Nine Mile Point Unit 1 reactors to 2049.
- *Uprate figures have been consistent and engineered*, not marketed: roughly 900 to 1,000 megawatts identified with completed engineering, concentrated at LaSalle, Limerick and Calvert Cliffs, with Byron and Braidwood in the plan.
- *Capacity revenue is now contracted, not hoped for*: the PJM auction for the 2028/2029 delivery year cleared at the $325 per megawatt-day ceiling on 14 July 2026.

---

## 7. Hidden signals

**The most important terminology shift** is from "behind the meter" to "front of the meter." In May 2025 co-location was the presumed structure. By August 2025: "what we're working on right now is all front of the meter." This is usually read as a negative — the premium structure did not work. I read it as a positive for durability and a negative for price: selling into the grid is a lower-friction, lower-ceiling business than selling a dedicated plant to a single hyperscaler at scarcity pricing.

**The second shift is the arrival of a new chief financial officer.** Dan Eggers led the finance commentary through November 2025; Shane Smith led it from March 2026. The change in what finance chooses to disclose is stark. Smith gave a three-year growth rate, a rolling growth commitment, a two-period free-cash-flow forecast, and — the most telling item — an explicit statement that the buyback is *excluded* from the growth target: "there is no benefit in the 20% base EPS CAGR from capital allocation for the share repurchase. So that is all upside." A finance chief who strips buyback accretion out of a headline growth number is not inflating the number.

**On capital allocation, the discipline language sharpened.** Smith, May 2026: "we won't make an ill-informed investment decision because we feel the money has got to go somewhere." Paired with a stated hurdle — growth projects at "double-digit unlevered returns" — and a stated willingness to buy stock instead when that hurdle is not met. That is the correct framework for a mid-build capital-intensive business, stated out loud.

**A subtle admission worth noticing.** In November 2025, asked whether the company would hold back capacity to capture scarcity pricing later, Dominguez said "we're not at a point where we're even entertaining the discussion of, hey, are we going to stop selling long term." Many investors value Constellation's uncontracted nuclear output as a free option on scarcity. Management has told you it intends to sell that option rather than hold it. That materially undercuts the most aggressive versions of the bull case.

---

## 8. Capital-allocation verdict

**Trajectory: Strengthening.**

The earnings base is larger, more diversified and better contracted than it was fifteen months ago. Revenue for the trailing twelve months reached $29.9 billion, up 23% year on year; operating cash profit margin runs at 27.6%, near the top of the peer cohort; net debt of $21.30 billion sits at 2.58 times operating cash profit, which is conservative against merchant-power peers running at five to seven-and-a-half times. Return on equity for the trailing twelve months is 20.1%.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing a position:** return on invested capital is 3.8% and return on capital employed 5.9%. Those are poor absolute returns. The kind explanation is that the Calpine capital base landed in full while only one quarter of Calpine earnings sits in the trailing numerator. The unkind explanation is that management paid a full price for a gas fleet and is telling you it was worth twice that. Which explanation is right will be visible in the returns line by mid-2027, and it is the difference between a compounding franchise and an expensive one. Do not size this position on the assumption that the kind explanation wins — size it so that either can be true.

**Economic moat: wide.** The moat type is a regulatory licence combined with scale-cost advantage. You cannot replicate the largest nuclear fleet in the United States at any price; new nuclear takes a decade and the replacement cost of even a new gas plant has risen from roughly $2,500 to roughly $3,000 per kilowatt on management's own account. Operating licences now run toward 2049 on filed applications. Federal nuclear production tax credit support, restated and strengthened in 2025 legislation, provides an effective revenue floor in the region of $40 to $44 per megawatt-hour on nuclear output — a genuine truncation of the downside, though far out of the money at today's power prices.

**Moat trend: stable, not widening.** Expanding operating margin argues for widening; a return on invested capital of 3.8% on a freshly stepped-up capital base does not permit that call yet. Revisit after two more quarters of combined-company reporting.

**Secular threat: none.** The structural force in this industry — electrification and artificial-intelligence-driven load growth — points toward this company, not away from it. The genuine risk is cyclical and political, not terminal: a digestion phase in data-centre capital spending, and a regulatory or political response to consumer electricity bills that caps the pricing the scarcity thesis depends on. The July 2026 auction clearing at an administratively set ceiling is exactly that risk made visible. A ceiling is protection for consumers and a lid on shareholders.

bull_thesis:
Vertiv is the equipment layer of the artificial-intelligence build-out, and the evidence that it holds real pricing power is now on the income statement rather than in the script. In the June 2026 quarter revenue reached $3,274 million, up 24% from a year earlier, while gross margin widened from 32.2% to 37.7% and adjusted operating margin — profit from operations before one-off items, as a share of sales — rose 410 basis points to 22.6%. A company giving away price to fill factories does the opposite. Management then raised full-year 2026 guidance for the third time in six months, to roughly $14.0 billion of sales at the midpoint, 30-32% organic growth, adjusted earnings per share of $6.65-$6.75 and adjusted free cash flow of $2.4-$2.6 billion, and guided the September quarter to 34-36% organic growth. At the May 2026 investor conference in Greenville the company reset its five-year frame upward, to 20-22% annual revenue growth and a 27% adjusted operating margin ambition for 2030, with capital spending held to 3-4% of sales and cash conversion of 95-100%.

The order book behind that is contractual rather than aspirational. Backlog last disclosed at $15.0 billion on 11 February 2026 was more than double the prior year and 57% higher than the September 2025 quarter, on orders up 252% year on year and a book-to-bill ratio — orders taken divided by revenue billed — of 2.9 times. Management defines backlog tightly: 'a binding purchase order... very often with advanced payment.' That definition is corroborated in cash, not just words: June-quarter adjusted free cash flow of $925 million, up 234%, was driven substantially by customer deposits taken against those orders. Named, dated deployments back it up — Hut 8 and Compass Data Centers, a Naval Postgraduate School installation around NVIDIA's DGX GB300 announced 23 July 2026, VisionBay.ai with Foxconn in Taiwan, Data4 in Frankfurt.

The obsolescence question that recurs every quarter has so far resolved in Vertiv's favour. Analysts have asked in turn whether in-row heat exchangers, microfluidic chip cooling, 800-volt direct-current architectures or warmer-running chips would strip Vertiv's content out of the rack. The falsifiable answer is dollars of Vertiv equipment per megawatt of data centre, and that number has gone up, from a $3.0-3.5 million range to $3.25-3.75 million as of the September 2025 quarter. Vertiv is now embedded in NVIDIA's Omniverse DSX design blueprint (1 June 2026) and in its 800-volt reference architecture — a switching cost that deepens each design cycle rather than eroding.

Capital discipline is the quiet part of the case and it is unusually good. The company repurchased $599.9 million of its own stock in fiscal 2024, when the shares traded at a small fraction of today's price, and has bought back nothing in 2025 or 2026 at three to five times that level, redirecting cash to bolt-on acquisitions that extend the thermal portfolio (Great Lakes and WeiLay in 2025, ThermoKey completed 12 June 2026, Strategic Thermal Labs announced 20 July 2026). Net debt of $146 million including leases against trailing adjusted earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation of about $2.52 billion means the balance sheet imposes no constraint at all; liquidity is $5.6 billion. The June-quarter revenue shortfall must prove to be the timing shift management described rather than the start of a conversion problem on the new prefabricated systems. bear_thesis:
The bear case does not require Vertiv to be a bad company. It requires only that the cycle turns and that the buyer, at today's price, has no early warning.

Start with what has been removed. From the 2026 reporting year Vertiv no longer discloses orders, order forecasts or backlog with quarterly results — announced in the June 2025 quarter, confirmed on the February 2026 call immediately after reporting the best order quarter in its history, and executed since. The June 2026 call gave no backlog figure and no book-to-bill ratio. The reasoning offered is that lumpy orders create 'unnecessary volatility... not beneficial to our investors.' Whatever the intent, the effect is that the single leading indicator for a business whose entire valuation rests on forward demand is now visible once a year, in the annual report. Every bullish claim about pipeline strength since February 2026 is unaudited management assertion.

Then look at what this company did the last time input costs ran ahead of a fixed-price order book. In fiscal 2022 revenue grew 13.8% while net income collapsed to $77 million and free cash flow turned to negative $264 million. Vertiv books binding purchase orders, often more than a year ahead of delivery, at prices struck today; copper, steel, transformers, switchgear components and freight are costs, so any inflation in them is a margin headwind, never a revenue tailwind. The 2025 tariff episode was a mild rerun — adjusted operating margin fell 110 basis points year on year in the June 2025 quarter, and the promise to be 'tariff neutral exiting 2025' slipped a quarter to the March 2026 quarter. The mechanism has been managed better; it has not been abolished.

The cracks in execution are new and they are in the strategically important part. June-quarter revenue of $3,274 million came in roughly 3% below what the street expected, attributed to 'multi-phase project execution and temporary supply chain dynamics' and a 'learning curve' on large interconnected projects. The converged, prefabricated products that justify the premium — OneCore and SmartRun — recognise revenue against project milestones, which is structurally lumpier and more working-capital hungry than shipping components. Organic growth in the quarter was 18%, down from 34% organic a year earlier, with five percentage points of the headline 24% coming from acquisitions and one from currency. Full-year guidance nonetheless calls for 30-32% organic, which requires a very sharp second-half reacceleration; the September-quarter guide of 34-36% organic is where that gets tested.

Europe is the clearest instance of narrative running ahead of numbers. Management called the region a 'coiled spring... uncoiling' in February 2026 while it ran down 14%, and it then ran down 29% organically in the March 2026 quarter. Guidance embeds a second-half return to growth that has not yet appeared.

Competition is not standing still. Eaton, Schneider Electric, ABB, nVent, Johnson Controls and Carrier all attack parts of this stack, and liquid cooling in particular has attracted a crowd. The hyperscaler customers are among the most sophisticated procurement organisations on earth, they are vertically integrating where they can, and customer concentration in a business where single orders now move a quarter cuts both ways.

What confirms the bear case: a September or December quarter where organic growth undershoots the 34-36% guide; any sequential decline in gross margin on rising revenue, which would say price is being conceded; the fiscal 2026 annual report showing backlog below $15 billion; a hyperscaler publicly pausing or re-phasing a build; or free cash flow deteriorating as customer deposits unwind into deliveries without being replaced by new ones. Priced adversely, this is not a small drawdown. The shares traded at $118.70 within the past twelve months and fell about 25% in four weeks into the July 2026 report on a 3% revenue miss — the market has already demonstrated how fast it will re-rate this name when conversion is questioned.

moderator_conclusion:
This is a good business at a price that leaves the buyer holding the wrong end of the asymmetry, so the answer is to wait for the wash-out rather than buy now — and to name the level rather than wave at one.

What is genuinely strong. The pricing-power test passes cleanly: gross margin widened about 550 basis points, from 32.2% to 37.7%, over the year to the June 2026 quarter while revenue grew 24%. Expanding margin on rising volume in a supply-constrained niche is the honest signature of pricing power; the opposite pattern would have told us volume was being bought with price. Adjusted operating margin rose 410 basis points to 22.6% and management raised full-year guidance for the third time in six months. The forensic record supports taking that at face value — seven earnings beats in seven quarters, free cash flow guided to $1.4 billion for 2025 and delivered at $1.89 billion, and, most tellingly, $599.9 million of stock repurchased in 2024 near the lows and nothing repurchased in 2025 or 2026 at three to five times the price. Buying low and declining to buy high is the reverse of what most management teams do with a hot share price, and it is the single best piece of evidence on capital discipline in the file. The balance sheet imposes no constraint at all: $146 million of net debt including leases against about $2.52 billion of trailing earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, with $5.6 billion of liquidity. Returns are rising, not falling — 20.8% on invested capital, 42.1% on equity — which is why we read the moat as narrow but widening rather than wide or eroding. And the terminal-value question is benign: artificial intelligence is this company's demand driver, not its displacer.

What holds us back, in order. First, the price. Our base-case sum-of-the-parts value is $315 a share against $273.35 today — about 15% of upside, and that already assumes 2027 revenue of roughly $16.9 billion at a 25.5% adjusted operating margin, which is not a conservative set of inputs. We are deliberately below the street's $357 consensus. Against that modest upside sits an adverse case at $128, built on the order book converting without being replaced and margin compressing under input costs and under-absorbed new capacity. That number is not theoretical: this stock printed $118.70 within the past twelve months, and fiscal 2022 shows what this business looks like when input costs run ahead of a fixed-price order book — revenue up 13.8%, net income $77 million, free cash flow negative $264 million. Roughly $42 of upside against roughly $145 of downside is not a shape we pay up for.

Second, the instrument panel has been removed. From the 2026 reporting year Vertiv no longer publishes orders or backlog quarterly. The $15 billion backlog and 2.9 times book-to-bill that the bullish commentary still quotes were last disclosed on 11 February 2026 and describe a quarter that closed more than seven months ago. Management pre-announced the change before the blowout, which is mitigating, and the stated rationale about lumpiness is coherent. The effect is not mitigated at all: the leading indicator that would tell us when this cycle turns is now visible once a year. That is a real reason to demand a wider margin of safety, not a smaller one.

Third, two live operating claims are unproven. Europe must swing from down 29% organically in the March quarter to growth in the second half of 2026, a turn management has been calling imminent since February while the number deteriorated. And the September quarter must deliver 34-36% organic growth immediately after a quarter that slipped 3% on what was described as a learning curve on large interconnected projects — the first time the converged, prefabricated strategy that justifies the premium has cost the company a number.

On timing: the forced selling already happened. The shares fell about 25% over four weeks into 29 July and have taken back roughly 23% in the four sessions since, closing at $273.35 today. Buying here is chasing the recovery, not the wash-out. The level we want is about $215 — printed nine days ago, on 29-30 July 2026 — where the same base case offers roughly $100 of upside against roughly $87 of downside and the arithmetic inverts. Failing that, a September-quarter print that clears 34-36% organic growth with Europe positive would let us raise the base case and justify paying closer to today's price on better information.

The value score sits at the same level as the execution call, and for once that is not a default: the discount to our own fair value is thin at 15%, and while the forensic quality is high and the moat is widening rather than melting, neither of those creates value at a price that has already been paid. Both scores are held at neutral. The catalyst position — that the investor conference and the June-quarter print have both already fired — carries no weight either way in this lane; dated-event asymmetry is another book's business, and a spent event on a clean franchise is neither a credit nor a penalty here.

# Vertiv Holdings Co (VRT) — a deep dive on management and the setup

growth plus share gain. Executive Chairman Dave Cote in the first quarter of 2025: "the digital
revolution is happening. It still has a long way to go." Chief Executive Gio Albertazzi anchored
everything to a five-year model presented at a November 2024 investor day: 15-17% growth for the
cloud and colocation segment, 12-14% for Vertiv. The proof points offered were backlog ($7.9 billion,
first quarter 2025) and a book-to-bill ratio of 1.4 times — book-to-bill compares orders taken to
revenue billed, so anything above 1.0 means the order book is growing faster than sales.

**Step two — "we are the connective tissue" (second half of 2025).** In the second quarter of 2025
management introduced a genuinely new idea: that the "grey space" (power and cooling) and the "white
space" (the racks and servers) are merging as rack densities climb into the hundreds of kilowatts.
This was not marketing filler; it became the strategic basis for the converged, prefabricated products
launched later. Services were elevated from a footnote to what Albertazzi called "one of Vertiv's
superpowers" in the third quarter of 2025.

**Step three — "we sell the whole data centre" (2026).** By the fourth quarter of 2025 the company had
named products behind the idea: OneCore, a complete data-centre building block sold in 12.5-megawatt
increments, and SmartRun, a prefabricated white-space system. Named deployments followed with Hut 8
and Compass Data Centers. By the first quarter of 2026 the language moved to capacity: new plants,
a doubling of chiller capacity in Italy by end-2026, a new Malaysian factory opened 1 July 2026, and
capital spending stepping from the historical 2-3% of sales to 3-4%.

**What was quietly dropped.** Two things. First, the 12-14% Vertiv growth model from November 2024 has
been overtaken and replaced — at the May 2026 investor conference the company reset to a 20-22%
five-year revenue growth rate and a 27% adjusted operating margin ambition for 2030. That is an upgrade,
not a retreat, but it means the original five-year model no longer serves as a check on the story.
Second, and far more consequential, **the orders and backlog disclosure was withdrawn.** Flagged in
the second quarter of 2025, confirmed in the fourth quarter of 2025 ("we believe that currently, the
best approach is to no longer report actual orders, orders forecast or backlog with quarterly
earnings"), and executed from the first quarter of 2026 onward. The second-quarter 2026 call gave no
backlog figure and no book-to-bill ratio.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Margin recovery once tariff costs are absorbed | Q2-Q3 2025 | Gross margin 32.2% (Q2 2025) → 37.7% (Q2 2026). Adjusted operating margin 18.5% → 22.6%, up 410 basis points | **Delivered, convincingly** |

**Where the story is richer than the trajectory justifies.** Europe. Management has described the
region as improving for three consecutive calls while it deteriorated from −4% to −29%. The promise
of a return to growth in the second half of 2026 is now embedded in guidance and is the single
unverified operating claim in the file.

**Where the story is poorer than the trajectory justifies.** Cash generation. Management understated
it repeatedly — guiding $1.4 billion in free cash flow for 2025 and delivering $1.89 billion; guiding
$6.02 in adjusted earnings per share for 2026 in February, raising to $6.35 in April, then to $6.70
in July. Three raises in six months is not a company straining to hit its numbers.

**The one genuine operating stumble.** Second-quarter 2026 revenue of $3,274 million grew 24% but
landed roughly 3% below what the street expected. Management attributed it to "minor timing shifts...
primarily driven by multi-phase project execution and temporary supply chain dynamics" — a "learning
curve" on large interconnected projects. The stock fell about 25% over four weeks into that print.
This is the first evidence that the converged, prefabricated strategy carries execution and revenue-
timing risk that the older component business did not: milestone-based revenue recognition on
multi-phase projects is lumpier by construction.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Rising, and increasingly specific.**

- *First quarter 2025* — confident but hedged on tariffs: "rather than speculate, we'll continue to
  focus on what we can't control" (a transcription slip for "can control"). Guidance ranges were
  *widened* to absorb tariff uncertainty.
- *Second quarter 2025* — the most defensive call in the set. Albertazzi conceded "some executional
  challenges in EMEA" and margin down 110 basis points year on year. Language turned to mitigation
  and cost.
- *Third quarter 2025* — the pivot back to offence. Cote: "this is a very strong quarter by any
  measure... I wonder what would have happened if we hadn't blown the doors off of every single
  metric." Note the irritation at the share-price reaction; the stock fell on a beat.
- *Fourth quarter 2025* — peak confidence, with the numbers to match: orders up 252% year on year,
  backlog doubling to $15 billion.
- *First quarter 2026* — Cote: "what we're seeing in customer conversations is different than 6
  months ago. The urgency has increased."
- *Second quarter 2026* — confidence maintained through a revenue miss; guidance raised across every
  line rather than trimmed.

There is no shift from offensive to defensive language. If anything the reverse: the defensive
vocabulary clustered in the middle of 2025, when tariffs and European execution were biting, and has
since been replaced by capacity, investment and content-per-megawatt.

**One tonal caution.** The rhetoric is consistently superlative — "the future has never been
brighter", "I'm more excited today than I've ever been", "insatiable, dare I say, demand". In a sector
where promoters live, this register is a standing flag. What defends Vertiv here is that the numbers
have so far exceeded the rhetoric rather than trailed it.

---

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Score: High.**

The pattern is unambiguous and one-directional: guide conservatively, raise repeatedly, deliver above
the raised number. Fiscal 2025 sales guidance went from 18% growth (April) to 24% (July) and landed at
27.7%. Fiscal 2026 adjusted earnings per share guidance went $6.02 (February) → $6.35 (April) →
$6.65-$6.75 (July). Free cash flow guidance for 2025 went to $1.4 billion and delivered $1.89 billion.
The screener records seven earnings beats out of seven quarters.

This is sandbagging, and it should be read as such — the *level* of guidance carries little
information, the *direction of revision* carries most of it. The single blemish is the tariff-neutrality
date, promised for the end of 2025 and re-promised for the end of the first quarter of 2026. They
missed the first date and hit the second.

The offsetting concern is not accuracy but **verifiability**. With orders and backlog withdrawn from
quarterly disclosure, the leading indicator that would confirm or contradict the guidance a year ahead
is now visible only once a year, in the annual report. An investor is being asked to take the
company's word on the one number that matters most.

---

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

**The recurring question is technological obsolescence, and it is asked every single quarter in a new
costume.** Amit Mehrotra of UBS put it plainly in the third quarter of 2025: "every three or four
months, there's some announcement or some innovation that gets everybody to question the entire thesis
around Vertiv's position." The specific threats raised across the calls: Amazon Web Services designing
its own in-row heat exchangers; Microsoft microfluidics cooling chips directly; 800-volt direct current
architectures eliminating power supply units; NVIDIA's Rubin-generation racks running warm enough to
skip chillers; competitors' stainless-steel chillers displacing coolant distribution units.

Management's answers have been substantive rather than evasive, and — importantly — checkable.
Albertazzi argued that microfluidics is still direct-to-chip liquid cooling and "preserves everything,
thermal chain... intact"; that 800-volt direct current plays to decades of Vertiv direct-current
experience; that warmer chips reduce chiller count but not the need for heat rejection, which is why
the company catalogued a "Trim Cooler". The falsifiable claim attached to these answers is content per
megawatt, and it has gone **up**, not down: from a $3.0-3.5 million range to $3.25-3.75 million as of
the third quarter of 2025, and Vertiv is now embedded in NVIDIA's Omniverse DSX reference blueprint
(announced 1 June 2026).

**Genuinely deflected.** Two topics. First, backlog margin — Chris Snyder of Morgan Stanley asked
directly in the second quarter of 2025 whether the margin embedded in backlog supports a fourth-quarter
recovery, and got "we do not go in those level of details." Second, orders guidance — Mehrotra pressed
on trailing-twelve-month orders in the second quarter of 2025 and was told "I would be guiding orders,
and that's not what we do."

**What analysts worried about that turned into bad news.** The margin pressure Snyder probed in the
second quarter of 2025 was real and lasted three quarters. The European weakness analysts pushed on
from the first quarter of 2025 got worse for a full year. Both were flagged by the sell side before
management conceded them.

**What analysts are not pressing hard enough on.** The working-capital shape of the new converged
business. Nigel Coe of Wolfe Research got closest in the first quarter of 2026, asking whether the
surge in customer deposits is a readable proxy for backlog growth; Chief Financial Officer Craig
Chamberlin's answer was "it is a way to look at backlog, but it's not entirely our read through."
Advance payments flatter free cash flow while orders are being taken and reverse when they are
delivered. Second-quarter 2026 free cash flow of $925 million, up 234%, is partly a deposit-timing
figure, not a steady-state one.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 **Orders and backlog disclosure withdrawn at the exact peak.** Announced in the second quarter of
2025, confirmed in the fourth quarter of 2025 immediately after reporting orders up 252% and a
book-to-bill of 2.9 times, effective from 2026. The stated reason — lumpiness causing "unnecessary
volatility... not beneficial to our investors" — is coherent, and the fact that it was pre-announced
before the blowout quarter is genuinely mitigating. The effect is not. The primary leading indicator
for this company is now dark between annual reports.

🔴 **Europe: three calls of improvement language against a worsening number.** "The coiled spring is
uncoiling" (fourth quarter 2025) was said while the region ran −14%, and it then ran −29% in the first
quarter of 2026.

🔴 **No insider buying on the open market.** Zero open-market purchases against 38 disposals totalling
about 271,000 shares. Recent Form 4 filings (25 June 2026) are dividend-equivalent accruals of a few
shares each; the 4 May 2026 disposals at $330.97 were tax withholding on vesting rather than
discretionary sales. So the disposals are less damning than the raw count suggests — but the absence
of buying at any point in a 130% share-price round trip is still an absence.

🔴 **The 2022 precedent is in this company's own accounts.** Revenue grew 13.8% in fiscal 2022 while
net income collapsed to $77 million and free cash flow went to **negative $264 million**. That was
input-cost and freight inflation running through a fixed-price order book. The mechanism that broke
Vertiv four years ago has not been legislated away; it has been managed better.

🔴 **Execution stumble on the new converged products.** The second-quarter 2026 revenue shortfall was
attributed to a "learning curve" on large interconnected projects — the first time the strategy that
justifies the premium has cost the company a number.

🟢 **Gross margin expanding while revenue accelerates.** From 32.2% in the second quarter of 2025 to
37.7% in the second quarter of 2026, on revenue up 24%. In a supply-constrained niche this is the
cleanest available evidence of pricing power. The opposite pattern — margin falling as revenue grows —
would have signalled that volume was being bought with price.

🟢 **Buybacks at the bottom, none at the top.** The company repurchased $599.9 million of stock in
fiscal 2024, when the shares traded at a fraction of today's price, and has repurchased **nothing** in
2025 or 2026 at three to five times that level. Cash has gone instead to bolt-on acquisitions
($1.18 billion in 2025: Great Lakes, WeiLay; then ThermoKey completed 12 June 2026 and Strategic
Thermal Labs announced 20 July 2026) and a token dividend of $0.0625 a quarter. This is the reverse of
the usual pattern and it is the strongest single piece of evidence on capital discipline.

🟢 **Balance sheet effectively unlevered.** Net debt of $146 million including finance leases at 30
June 2026 against trailing twelve-month adjusted earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and
amortisation of about $2.52 billion — roughly 0.06 times. Excluding leases the company is in a small
net cash position, which is how the second-quarter release describes it. Liquidity $5.6 billion.

🟢 **Named, dated, checkable deployments rather than memoranda of understanding.** Hut 8 and Compass
Data Centers (fourth quarter 2025), the Naval Postgraduate School NVIDIA DGX GB300 installation
(23 July 2026), VisionBay.ai/Foxconn in Taiwan and Data4 in Frankfurt (second quarter 2026 call).
Backlog is defined tightly: "a binding purchase order... very often with advanced payment."

🟢 **Capacity is being added against demand, with disclosed sites and dates.** Johor, Malaysia opened
1 July 2026; Tognana, Italy chiller capacity to double by end-2026 with a testing laboratory in early
2027. Management is explicit that it runs 20-25% deliberate slack in factory loading.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

**Terminology.** The vocabulary moved from components ("thermal", "power") to systems ("connective
tissue", "converged", "prefabricated", "time to token") and finally to the customer's own unit of
account — dollars of Vertiv content per megawatt of data centre. That last shift matters because it
converts an obsolescence debate into an arithmetic one, and the arithmetic has moved in Vertiv's
favour.

**How competition is discussed.** In the third quarter of 2025 Albertazzi made a striking observation:
comparing liquid cooling today with eighteen months earlier, he saw "a better delineation of the
competitive landscape... more consolidated, more rational players not bad." A market leader welcoming
consolidation among its rivals is describing an industry where price competition is easing — which is
exactly what the gross-margin line then did.

**Capital allocation language hardened.** In the second quarter of 2025 acquisitions were "an important
element". By the first quarter of 2026 Albertazzi said the company has "no reticence in cutting bigger
checks when that's needed". Deal sizes are not being disclosed ("we didn't give any of the sizes, but
if they were materially impactful to us, we would have"), which is defensible for bolt-ons but removes
a check on the return being earned on $1.18 billion of 2025 acquisition spend.

**New voices.** Chief Financial Officer David Fallon retired, announced on the third-quarter 2025 call
with Craig Chamberlin succeeding him from the fourth quarter of 2025. A new Chief Procurement Officer,
Frieda He, joined 5 May 2026 with a mandate on supply-chain resilience and cost. Chamberlin is
noticeably more forthcoming on the mechanics — his answers on incremental margins, customer deposits
and product mix are more concrete than his predecessor's, and he volunteered the constraint that
incremental margins are being guided at the low end of the 30-35% range because of the investment ramp.
That is a chief financial officer describing a cost, not selling a story.

**One arithmetic tell.** The second-quarter 2026 revenue of $3,274 million included five percentage
points of growth from acquisitions and one from currency. Organic growth was 18%, against 34% organic
in the same quarter a year earlier. Headline growth of 24% is being increasingly assisted by
acquisitions. Full-year guidance still calls for 31% organic, which requires a sharp reacceleration in
the second half — the third-quarter guide of 34-36% organic is where that gets tested.

---

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT

**Trajectory: STRENGTHENING.**

Returns are rising, not falling: return on invested capital of 20.8% and return on equity of 42.1% on
a trailing twelve-month basis, with gross margin up about 550 basis points and adjusted operating
margin up 410 basis points year on year. Growth capital spending is stepping up from 2-3% to 3-4% of
sales into visible, dated capacity additions, funded entirely from a free cash flow line running at
$2.4-2.6 billion for 2026 with essentially no net debt. Buybacks were executed at the low and stopped
at the high.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing.** Not whether the franchise is good — it
demonstrably is — but that **the one number that would tell you when this cycle turns is no longer
published quarterly.** Vertiv's entire forward visibility rests on a backlog last disclosed at $15
billion on 11 February 2026 and on management's unaudited assurance since. The company is priced for
the order book to keep compounding, and the buyer has surrendered the instrument that would give early
warning if it does not. Size for a business whose demand signal you can only inspect once a year.

**Economic moat: NARROW, and WIDENING.** The moat type is switching costs layered over scale and
intangible engineering assets. The switching costs are real and getting deeper: an installed base
served by a global field-service organisation, early involvement in customer project design ("early
involvement in project technology and in project planning further drives our above-market growth",
third quarter 2025), and now inclusion in NVIDIA's reference architecture for both 800-volt direct
current power and the Omniverse DSX design blueprint. Scale shows up as the ability to deliver
gigawatt-class programmes on a schedule, which is the binding constraint for every hyperscaler.

It is narrow rather than wide because the competitive set is formidable and well funded — Eaton,
Schneider Electric, ABB, nVent, Johnson Controls and Carrier all attack parts of this stack, and the
liquid-cooling entrants are numerous. It is widening rather than eroding because the evidence points
that way: returns rising, gross margin expanding on accelerating revenue, content per megawatt guided
up rather than down, and the leader's own read that the field is consolidating toward "more rational
players."

**Secular threat: manageable.** The structural forces that impair terminal value elsewhere do not
point at this business. Artificial intelligence is Vertiv's demand driver, not its displacer; there is
no channel shift, no reimbursement compression, no disintermediation path. The genuine risk here is
**cyclical, not secular** — a hyperscaler capital-spending digestion phase that empties the order book
for a year or two. That distinction is the whole investment question: the terminal value looks intact,
the near-term earnings base does not look safe. Consequently the shares are neither a fear-print
mispricing nor a value trap; at 41.9 times trailing enterprise value to earnings before interest, tax,
depreciation and amortisation they are a high-quality franchise carrying a full price and a genuine
cyclical drawdown risk.

TE Connectivity is a component manufacturer that has quietly become the second-largest supplier of the connectors and power hardware that artificial-intelligence data centers and modernised electricity grids cannot be built without - and it is priced as though it were still mainly a car-parts company. Start with the demand evidence, which is unusually hard for a technology story. Orders - the leading indicator, since they are placed before revenue is recognised - have risen for five consecutive quarters, from $4.5 billion in the June-2025 quarter to a record $5.7 billion in the June-2026 quarter, up 27% year over year, with double-digit growth in every single business and every region. Digital Data Networks orders are up over 70% year-to-date. This is not a projection; it is signed demand already on the books.

The artificial-intelligence business has beaten its own public target early. Revenue from these applications went from $300 million in fiscal 2024 to over $900 million in fiscal 2025, and by the June-2026 quarter the company had reached the $3 billion annual run rate it laid out at its November-2025 investor day - ahead of schedule. Terrence Curtin, the chief executive, in July 2026: 'the $3 billion we laid out, we're ahead of, and that has continued to shift left.' Importantly, about one-third of that revenue is power connectivity rather than data connectivity, and power content rises as rack architectures move toward 800 volts.

The second engine is the electricity grid. The energy business grew 33% organically in the June-2026 quarter on utilities replacing ageing infrastructure and on the power build-out feeding data centers. The $2.3 billion Richards Manufacturing purchase completed in fiscal 2025 bought a leading position in North American underground distribution equipment, and management says it is running ahead of the original plan.

Profitability is improving while all this happens, which is the real test. Adjusted operating margin rose from 20.0% to 22.0% year over year. Industrial Solutions margins expanded by roughly 400, 300 and 500 basis points in three of the last four quarters to reach 22.8%. Heath Mitts, the chief financial officer, has promised 'roughly 30% flow-through' - meaning thirty cents of every incremental sales dollar reaches operating profit - on every single call, has been challenged on it by analysts repeatedly, and delivered about 36% in the June-2026 quarter.

The moat claim is specific rather than generic. Connectors are designed into a customer's architecture years before volume, so displacing an incumbent means requalifying the platform. Curtin on 800-volt data centers, July 2026: 'I don't see new entrants coming in because this is a simultaneous equation of trade-offs and constraints between the data and the power equation when you're at the rack.' Corroborating evidence from outside the company: reports of coordinated connector price increases of 5% to 15% from TE Connectivity, Amphenol and Molex effective July 2026 - that is a concentrated market exercising pricing power, not a commodity market.

Management has earned trust the hard way. It guided and beat both sales and adjusted earnings per share in four consecutive quarters (guided $4.55B/$2.27 and delivered $4.75B/$2.44; guided $4.5B/$2.53 and delivered $4.67B/$2.72; guided $4.7B/$2.65 and delivered $4.74B/$2.73; guided $5.0B/$2.83 and delivered $5.16B/$2.94). Cash conversion has run above 100%, free cash flow was over $3 billion in fiscal 2025, roughly all of it is returned to shareholders, the dividend was raised 10% in March 2026, and diluted share count has fallen from 305 million to 293 million in seven quarters. Net debt is $4.39 billion against roughly $4.85 billion of trailing operating cash earnings - under one times.

The re-rating mechanism is the mix. In the June-2026 quarter Industrial Solutions and Transportation Solutions each printed exactly $2.58 billion of sales - the first time they have been equal. Industrial grew 21.9%, Transportation 6.7%. The market has valued this company at a wide discount to Amphenol and Hubbell because more than half of it was automotive; from here, more than half of it is not. If the multiple simply migrates part-way toward the peer group as that becomes undeniable, the shares work without a single new assumption about demand.

Conditions that must hold: hyperscaler capital spending does not pause through fiscal 2027; copper cost increases continue to be passed through within a quarter or two; global auto production holds near the guided 88 million units; and the $1.4 billion Astrodyne TDI purchase integrates as cleanly as Richards did.
bear_thesis:
The bear case is not that this is a bad company - it plainly is not - but that you are being asked to pay a full price for peak conditions in a business whose two growth engines share one customer, at a moment when its main raw material is at an all-time high.

First, the concentration is worse than the segment chart suggests. Digital Data Networks and the energy business are both now explicitly levered to the same demand: data-center construction. Management said so in July 2026 - 'Our AI opportunity extends beyond the rack. Data center build-outs are driving significant investment across the power infrastructure.' Curtin has been equally clear about who the buyer is: 'the bigger driver of growth for us is the hyperscalers that have their custom TPUs and GPUs.' Combined, these two businesses generated well over $1 billion of the quarter's $2.58 billion of Industrial revenue and essentially all of the growth. A digestion pause by a handful of buyers - not a collapse, just a pause - removes the entire growth story at once. Order books do not protect you here: orders can be rescheduled, and a record backlog built during a capital-spending boom is exactly the backlog that gets pushed out.

Second, copper. TE Connectivity is a connector maker; copper is a cost, not a revenue tailwind, and it hit roughly $14,000 per tonne on the London Metal Exchange on 4 August 2026 - a record. Management admits feeling it (January 2026: 'as the spot market goes up, we feel that... yes, we're feeling it right now') and passes it through, but pass-through revenue carries no profit. The proof is already in the accounts: gross margin has fallen from 37.2% in the December-2025 quarter to 36.8% and then 35.6% - about 1.6 percentage points of compression in two quarters while revenue grew. If copper stays here and the pass-through lags by even one quarter in a slowing order environment, the 30%-plus flow-through promise breaks, and that promise is load-bearing for the entire earnings model.

Third, the optical displacement risk is real and now conceded. Pressed for three consecutive quarters, Curtin finally said it plainly in July 2026: 'we are not a major player in scale-out. When you think about scale-out, which is almost all optical today, we have a limited position there.' Roughly two-thirds of the artificial-intelligence revenue is data connectivity - copper. The RAM Photonics purchase in April 2026 is a foothold, not a position. If scale-up networking inside the rack follows scale-out toward optical faster than management expects, the fastest-growing part of this company is displaced by a technology it does not lead. TE Connectivity is also the acknowledged number two: an analyst put a competitor at roughly three times its artificial-intelligence revenue in October 2025 and management did not dispute the figure.

The company has committed close to $4 billion to acquisitions in two years - $2.3 billion for Richards Manufacturing (about 5.8 times its roughly $400 million of sales) and $1.4 billion for Astrodyne TDI announced 22 July 2026 (about 5.6 times its 'more than $250 million' of sales). Buying other companies for more than the market charges for your own is only accretive if synergies are quantified, and on five calls they never were. The market registered its objection: the shares fell 6.9% on 22 July 2026, the day of a beat on both lines with record orders, and the decline was attributed to the Astrodyne announcement rather than the results.

Fifth, the automotive half is not a source of support. Global auto production is guided at roughly 88 million units, 'down slightly,' with Western regions declining every quarter for over a year and growth carried entirely by Asia. Transportation Solutions grew 6.7% in the June-2026 quarter against Industrial's 21.9%. In a genuine recession this half of the company shrinks, and it is still half.

Sixth, the multiple is not a floor. The peer group - Amphenol at roughly 24 times enterprise value to operating cash earnings, Hubbell at 21 times, Eaton at 32 times - is at cycle-peak valuations on the same artificial-intelligence enthusiasm. A capital-spending scare de-rates the whole complex together, and TE Connectivity's discount does not exempt it. There is no structural floor under the shares: this is a company with net debt, not net cash, no deal terms, and no asset backing that supports a liquidation value anywhere near the market price. Tangible asset value is roughly $3.9 billion against a $62.6 billion market capitalisation.
